utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Please continue, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I want to move on now from the objectivity and impartiality of your reports and ask you about some of your substantive criticisms of the Prosecution's evidence. One of the main criticisms we've heard you testify about and that's throughout your reports are the assumptions by the Prosecution pathologists that the vast majority of gun-shot and other injuries occurred in life and that these injuries were or contributed to the cause of death. Now, the Prosecution experts explained these assumptions very clearly in their reports, didn't they, Professor?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they explained the theory in the introduction, as John Clark wrote that and everyone else wrote that in an identical way, copy-and-paste system, they explained how difficult and impossible it was to determine which wounds were created ante-mortem and which post-mortem on the material that is skeletised, that was exhumed and so on and so forth, and that is what is absolutely acceptable, and I said that all of that is acceptable from a professional aspect. On the other hand, they are now explaining their assumptions, the assumption that those people had to have been in some way killed because there are corpses. The second assumption was that the injuries in that case had to have been ante-mortem, and then in the end, they refer to anthropological findings as the only findings that could indicate that something was inflicted ante-mortem. So I am actually criticising the generally accepted assumption, and that applies to all, not just the anthropologist but also the forensics experts who conducted the autopsies, the general assumption that all of the injuries were inflicted ante-mortem, that all those -- all the corpses died from gun-shot wounds, and that there was a very small number where the cause of death was not determined, where they could not determine it, as there were no indications of any kind, markings. I'm pointing that out because in this material this was something that should have been put conditionally, and those parameters should have been presented objectively that would speak to wounds having been caused on the head as the cause of death but with the proviso that it could have been assumed that such a person could have sustained those injuries post-mortem, but that the cause of death was actually injury of the chest --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor -- Professor, let me --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- they did have such cases --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let me stop you there --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right, all right, all right. I understand. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I just wanted to make sure the assumptions were very clear. You understood that these assumptions were being relied on?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was participating [as interpreted] that the whole time in my reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. And you'd agree that the Court has a lot of other evidence on how those bodies ended up in those graves; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. So it's up to the Court to decide whether those assumptions of the Prosecution experts is reasonable or not; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely agree and I wrote it down, that it was up to the Court to determine that. But it's not up to the forensics experts, myself, Clark, Lawrence, and others, to say that the victims were killed deliberately by execution and that injuries were inflicted deliberately. That is not up to the expert; it's up to the expert to explain how the injuries were caused, in which parts of the body, and for the person conducting the autopsy to describe them in detail and to link them with possible causes. But it's up to the Court, through all the presented evidence other than the exhumations and the autopsies, through all the presented evidence to establish whether that victim or that person who was found killed, was it -- were they killed, were they executed, or was this death caused by some other way. So for that reason I said that this was up to the Court to include those elements, or rather, to decide and not up to the experts who were providing very free conclusions. Allow me, just permit me to tell you this, let me just give you an example so that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- well, Haglund speaks about injury --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- let me stop you there --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Just come back to my question. It's the Court's role to decide whether the assumptions of the Prosecution experts are reasonable or not; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: All right. Let's -- I want to have a look at an example of one of your analyses of a Prosecution autopsy report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 1D25489 in e-court, page 193 in the English, 180 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And what you'll see, Professor, is this is your analysis of a body from the Ravnice grave.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just find that. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: It's your early report from the Popovic case, Professor, the big one.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, yes, yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And we see here that on the fluoroscopy there was one sharp-pointed copper jacket and some various other metal fragments --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fragments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes. And --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- your comment is that there are no grounds to maintain that these are gun-shot injuries. Is it your expert opinion, Professor, that when the fluoroscope showed a sharp-pointed copper jacket in the body of this individual, there are no grounds to maintain that this person has suffered a gun-shot injury? That's your analysis of this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am an expert for that and that's why I'm telling you now. Look at this case, a skeletonised corpse with some skeletonised parts, a copper jacket and some metal fragments were found. So the question here is if these metal parts are part of a projectile that pass through the soft tissue of the body or they were there subsequently from some other body or from that area, they reached those described parts. My objection is the description of the injuries are unfounded by the findings in the main injuries here because below the fluoroscopy it says: "Main injuries: "Fractured blade of the left scapula with multiple bone defects. Fractured 4th to 10th right ribs with many parts that are missing. Fractured 5, 6, and 12 thoracic-vertebral bodies. Fracture of the right radius ..." Yes, these are fractures and by some logic of things they could be created by a gun-shot wound, but based on such a description by any forensics experts, regardless if there are metal fragments there or not in the surrounding area, cannot conclude whether these are direct or indirect fractures, whether those fractures were created by those parts of the projectile or they were created in some other way. What -- now we're going back to the beginning what you asked me about. I don't have one element here on the basis of which I could conclude that these are fractures caused by gun-shot wounds and that they were inflicted ante-mortem. This is what I was talking about. What is presented here is a finding which is not that detailed with certain radiographic evidence and the cause of death is said to be injury of the chest and abdomen inflicted by fire-arm with a finding that is seen here. Somebody could draw a conclusion or they could say yes, gun-shot wounds were found, but I know that this man was stabbed in the heart with a knife which is not identified or that he was strangled. How could I know that when that is not described ante-mortem? And this is precisely what I'm talking about. And if I may digress, if you permit me, Mr. Mitchell. Three weeks ago --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let me just come back to -- that -- we're not talking about just metal fragments, we're talking about a sharp-pointed copper jacket inside this person. That couldn't have gotten there without causing an injury, could it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And where is that sharp copper jacket found? Where is it located? I'm asking you: Where is it? It's just mentioned here, but where is it found in the body? Do you understand what I'm saying to you now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying, Professor --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- what it says here, one sharp-pointed copper jacket --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, I'm just challenging the reasonableness of your assertion that there are no grounds to maintain that these are gun-shot injuries when there are quite obviously some very good grounds to maintain that these are gun-shot injuries because there's a sharp-pointed copper jacket inside this person; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your legal formulation why you are disputing what I'm saying because what needs to be proved is that it is so. All I want to do is to present evidence to the Tribunal and to you that this finding is not absolute proof for your assertion. In my comment I said that, like in the majority of cases, a conclusion is disputable and it's not a founded, grounded finding to state that this was inflicted by a fire-arm. This copper jacket that was identified and that I know also came from a projectile -- but I'm asking you where was it found? Was it embedded in the bone or in some remnant of soft tissue and so on and so forth? Therefore, I know that such a metal jacket can arrive secondarily if bodies are piled one on top of another. This is what I'm talking about. So I'm not criticising the findings; I'm just saying that this is an incomplete finding for such an assertion, and the Trial Chamber would have all the elements to prove everything. Would you like me to give you an example? I just need three seconds without being interrupted. Do you know that Tutankhamen, when they placed his body in an x-ray in 1980 or 1976 for the first time, they established a fracture on the right occipital bone, and only two years ago when they placed the same body of Tutankhamen under a scanner and in an MRI, it was noted that there were no fractures of the skull. But at that time in London they asserted that in 1976, I don't know, whenever the first time he was x-rayed, is that there was a fracture of the skull and that this was an injury sustained in fighting, which is not true. So an x-ray is something that is subject to a very serious discussion and it should be taken very seriously. So I have a radiographical finding here saying that a sharp-pointed copper jacket is there. Where? How was it positioned? This is what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Right. Let's move on, Professor. You've been very critical of the Prosecution's autopsy reports quite generally, so I just want to take a couple of minutes and ask you about your own procedures and standards, Professor, that you implemented when you were asked to examine some bodies in Eastern Bosnia in 1992. You were part of a Serbian team that went to Zvornik on the 16th of May, 1992, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you went there because the Serbian Ministry of Health received a request from the investigating judge in Zvornik to identify 150 bodies that had been collected in Karakaj and Bratunac; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you're asking me about something that happened many years ago, I assume -- yes, yes, we were there but I don't know any details. But please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Well --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our professor was heading the team at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, Professor Samuilo Pejakovic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Samuilo Pejakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes. So you went to Karakaj on the 16th of May, 1992, and examined 16 bodies in plastic bags in the slaughter-house; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you did a basic examination for age, sex, and any characterisations that were useful for identifying these individuals?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you found that four of them had identification on them, identifying them as Muslims?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me that I absolutely don't know the details. I did provide a statement about it, but I don't recall the details. Perhaps you can just give me some information and everything that is under my signature I can confirm. I know that that was so, but I don't remember the particulars. This was 20 years or more ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. So you did a basic examination but you didn't do an autopsy on any of these bodies, did you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. So there's no formal autopsy report at all?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think there are some photographs. I think I even showed some photographs that we made for the purposes of identification, and nothing more than that, to one of your investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, Dr. or Professor Pejakovic went down to Bratunac to look at the 100-odd bodies in the primary school there, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he went there alone. From what he told me or actually told all of us, this was in the gym of the elementary school all together. Since it was summer, the putrefaction was very pronounced so there was concern that the infection would spread. So then he himself said that that should be buried right away in order to prevent the possibility of infection spreading. This is what I remember in this elementary school, but we as a team who were with Professor Pejakovic, we did not go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes. And so again this Serbian team sent over, didn't do any autopsies. Professor Pejakovic said: Just put these bodies in a grave?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- yes, yes, yes, precisely. I think that when you asked me that in order for everything to be clear to everyone it was -- I don't know exactly which date it was. All of that began in a chaotic way. Some actions began to happen and we got some information and requests to help people over there in the field, for something to be done there - that was still Yugoslavia, the jurisdictions were with the republican ministries. So then there was some kind of military jurisdiction and then police jurisdiction, then the investigating judge would give an order: Can you as experts help us? What should we do with all of those people we found dead on the streets? And I say: Well, first of all we have to take -- see how many of them there were, photograph them, try to identify them, and then bury them. That's how it was exactly, and then they said: Well, there are a few dead people over there, can you do something? So we said: All right. Let's see if we can photograph them. If we can just take the basic parameters, if it is a male, a female, what is the height, the length. And then they said: Well, in some school over there near Bratunac, there is a large number of bodies. Can something be done over there? I said: We cannot go there. We don't know what this is about. We have to have a court order to do autopsies. You cannot do an autopsy without a court order. Perhaps some external examination can be done simply so that people are informed what it's all about and so on and so forth. So that we -- all of that was finished in the course of one day and we did not do any autopsies there. The only thing we did was we photographed -- we photographed those people in that place and we examined them. We even found those identification documents, but I don't recall the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. The point is you and your colleagues were asked to look at these bodies and did no autopsy reports at all, no description of the mechanism of injury, no determination of cause of death, nothing like that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, at least I'm -- not that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, you'd agree, wouldn't you, that even if we accept your criticisms of the Prosecution's autopsy reports - which we don't - you'd agree that having an autopsy report with a short description and some clearly defined assumptions is infinitely preferable to having no autopsy report at all; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally, in normal circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you now about your evidence regarding the enrichment of the graves. And I want to deal first with what you said about Professor Wright's evidence on this point. You said in your testimony on Monday at transcript 41752 that Professor Wright could not rule out the possibility that the graves were enriched. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you said that Dr. Lawrence also couldn't rule out the possibility that the graves were enriched?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I remember and as far as my notes contain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, Professor, you're correct about Dr. Lawrence. Dr. Lawrence did say at transcript 22486 that he thought the variation in decomposition was probably explained by the location of the mass grave, but he accepted that he couldn't ascertain the time since death and so there were alternative possibilities available. And then he stated on three separate occasions that this was actually Professor Wright's area of expertise and that these questions should be put to him. Now, you're a forensic pathologist, Professor, do you accept - as Dr. Lawrence did - that the question of whether the graves are enriched is actually an archaeological question?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know what? I told you right away the school that I belong to as a forensic physician. I don't think that Professor Lawrence and I went through the same sort of schooling. As a forensic pathologist, I can assess whether there was enrichment of the grave primarily based on the decomposition of the body. The fact of the matter is that an archaeologist would have specific knowledge relative to the exploration of terrain, digging up the terrain, different types of soil, et cetera, on the basis of which they can draw the conclusion as to whether something was added at a later date. As a forensic expert, I find this sort of information important in order to establish what sort of decomposition can be found on the bodies in the grave and whether there is a presence of putrefaction in the grave which may point to a variation in times of death or times of interment. So in a way I believe myself to be more competent in that field than the archaeologist who will have a more narrow view of expertise. I have to have both his reports and the autopsist's report in order to be able to establish that. I do agree that the archaeologist would be able to establish whether it's a primary or a secondary grave on the basis of artefacts found in another locality, but I do assert that it is up to the forensic pathologist to determine these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: But you'd agree that on the specific question of whether there is a single hole exhumed and a single deposit within that hole is a question of archaeology?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question should be formulated this way: Is there anything in the hole or is there nothing? If a biological matter was buried there, a man, an animal, a plant, in that case other specialities would be involved in the investigation other than the archaeologist. If we're talking about the mass graves where bodies were interred, the archaeologist is there to establish the boundaries, the parameters of the grave, to determine the features of the terrain, whether anything was subsequently enlarged or not, et cetera. But without our forensic examination of the position of the body, body parts, et cetera, nothing much can be done. It's up to us. This is how we were taught and this is how we did things. The archaeologist is a part of the auxiliary staff in an investigation involving a mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, let me be a little bit more specific then. When the archaeologist is examining the grave and looks at the changes in soil structure and whether or not that specific location has been disturbed on one occasion or more than one occasion, that is the role of the archaeologist, isn't it, to look specifically at the grave itself and see whether that ground was disturbed once or more than one time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My experience in the field shows that the best results are achieved when the archaeologist begins to explore the space of the grave, and when alongside forensic experts and technicians bodies are removed and the surface beneath the corpses is explored and once the grave is fully emptied, the archaeologist is to explore the grave-site again. And so this is how it is best to approach the investigation of a grave where more than one body was recovered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, Professor, you said that it was Professor Wright's evidence that he could not exclude that the Glogova 1 grave was enriched. Let me read you what Professor Wright said on the 1st of December, 2011, at transcript 22313. And he was asked by Mr. Karadzic whether he found any graves that were enriched. And he said: "No. I understand the question and what you mean by 'enriched.' I did not see any graves which I interpreted as having been opened up for the purpose of depositing more bodies ..." And then he went on and specifically said: "I didn't see it at Glogova. I didn't see it at any of the graves that are attributed to the Srebrenica event, but one of those graves that we're talking about I did see in Bosnia but it was from 1992 killings ..." So Professor Wright actually testified the exact opposite of what you said, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: There's not much to clarify, Professor. You said he couldn't rule out that the graves were enriched. And Professor Wright very categorically said: "I didn't see it at any of the graves that are attributed to the Srebrenica event ..."

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if we're talking about the same thing. Professor Wright said that he could not rule out that some of the graves were enriched at a later point. I don't know what the transcript says. I listened to him say when he said that he could not rule it out. But regardless of it all, what Dusan Janc wrote in his report confirms what I'm saying now, i.e., that there were additional deposits of bodies in some of the graves --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: We're going --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- which precisely rules out --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- come to -- well, we're going to come to that shortly, Professor. So Professor Wright testified that for the graves he exhumed he didn't see any evidence that they had been opened up and enriched, and that was the same testimony that Mr. Fredy Peccerelli gave about Lazete 1 grave at transcript 22741, where he said that there was no evidence that Lazete 1 had been enriched either.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about Peccerelli.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You say in your August 2009 report that you found Mr. Peccerelli's report on Lazete 1 correct and acceptable. So you would agree that his testimony that there was no evidence that that grave had been enriched is also correct and acceptable, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And Dr. Haglund, who led the exhumations at Branjevo, Lazete 2A and 2B, and Cerska, was asked about this same issue by Mr. Karadzic at transcript 23913. And he said: "No, because most of these graves hadn't been added to. They were -- bodies were taken out, not more bodies put in or put on other bodies ..." And then he goes on: "I saw no indication of bodies having been there from previous wars or previous burials. That didn't show up in what our findings were." And then at transcript 23914 he said: "It's become much more clear since then that we had little to go on at that time. But when you have remains in a grave and you have one person on the bottom, one person in the middle, and another person on the top and these people are all wrapped around him because they're not layered at all, then you know that these people were dumped in that grave about the same time." So, Professor, you've got the leaders of the Prosecution's exhumation teams from 1996, 1998, 1999, 2000, all saying that there is no evidence in the graves that they exhumed, there's no evidence that those graves were enriched. So you'd agree that those experts who led those exhumations are in the best position to make that determination, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They perhaps are in a position to view these matters; however, from individual analysis that I conducted, this is not what follows. Regardless of them having given these final opinions and findings, they are not what follows from the state of matters. If you find bodies with varied stages of decomposition in a single grave, that most certainly indicates different times of death or times of interment. Now, the evidence of Dusan Janc states precisely that, namely that bodies were put in at different times. And my starting point was the statement by Dusan Janc. It is a completely legitimate conclusion to draw, just as they said that it was not up to me to conclude that -- that because according to them there was enough evidence -- according to me there was evidence, and according to them, that there were different times of interment of these people. We could not have buried 300 people in a single day, so it had to have been done at different times. However, it wasn't just their evidence that I analysed. I examined the individual analyses based on which they drew their conclusions, and I saw that errors were made. I saw that opinions were relatively unsubstantiated by findings, just as I indicated the case at Ravnice. There is a finding there but I don't know how to interpret it --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- this is the point that I'm making. Therefore, skeletonisation -- let me finish. Mummification. So skeletonisation, when there is no soft tissue; mummification, when the tissue is dried; saponification are other degrees of putrefaction. When all these are found in a single location, in answer to a question -- just as Lawrence said, that this reflected the degree of putrefaction in the pit itself -- now, in answer to the question as to whether this can explain the time of death and whether it can point to possible different times of death and different times of interment, he agreed with that possibility. He did not rule out the possibility. So I'm talking as a forensic expert.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 13, although I see that there is an indication that it should be repeated, the witness said that these three degrees of putrefaction were found in a single grave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, you keep coming back to Dusan Janc's corrigendum, so why don't we look at that now. It's Exhibit D1975. Let me be very clear, Professor. We don't contest that the Glogova grave contained bodies from the Vuk Karadzic school in Bratunac, from Potocari, Konjevic Polje, and one truckload along the grave -- sorry, along the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road. But the point you're making is that those bodies were deposited at different times; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what follows from the supplement -- or rather, I'm sorry, from the corrigendum to his report. This is what follows from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, if you look at that corrigendum, it doesn't say anywhere that those bodies were deposited at a different time, does it? This is your assumption. If you look at the second bullet point, it says: "The bodies of individuals from locations other than the Kravica warehouse were also taken to the Glogova mass graves ..." There is absolutely nothing about that happening subsequent to when the Kravica warehouse bodies were put there, is there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And when were the bodies taken over there from the Kravica warehouse? At the same time as these others that were brought by trucks? I'm asking you. What is the conclusion when he says "and along the road a truckload of bodies"? So what does it mean to bring another truckload of bodies? They were already interred and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, let me stop you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- subsequently brought over. How do you interpret it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, I'll tell you exactly how we interpret it. You need to look at those three witness statements, don't you, to tell exactly when those bodies were put in the grave?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So may I then know what these witnesses said? I only have this report. Bodies of individuals from locations other than the Kravica warehouse were also taken to the Glogova mass graves. So they were taken or brought there. It is a lasting activity which has a certain duration. These other locations include -- and now it goes on to say Bratunac up to 80 bodies, Potocari, Konjevic Polje, Bratunac is over here, Potocari is over there, do you think it was all done in the space of one day or perhaps later?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, Professor, let me stop you --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- his report which is based also on --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- before you speculate too much, those three witnesses make it very clear that those bodies --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not speculating.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, those three witnesses make it very clear that those bodies were put in the Glogova grave while it was opened in the period from approximately 14 to 17 July, which would mean that Professor Wright's testimony that the Glogova grave wasn't enriched by a later deposit is accurate; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not base my opinion on witness statements. How would Professor Wright in that case account for the different degrees of putrefaction? He asserts that there was no later enrichment of the grave, there were no later deposits of bodies. Then my question would be: If all of them were buried at the same time, how is it possible to bury this amount of bodies in the space of three days in the same grave and have different degrees of putrefaction? This means that either times of death were different or that they were brought from different areas, which is confirmed here as the case. So if someone was buried in that grave on the 15th of July, how did the body come to be skeletonised unless the body -- unless the person died six months earlier. So I'm telling you as a forensics expert, not just as an archaeologist. So the witness statement is something that I can use only to establish the approximate time of death. However, what I have been arguing all this time on the basis of documents that I received as an expert is that the victims that were recovered in these specific locations were not buried in the space of five days, between the 10th or the 19th of July, 1995, but that there were among them those who died much, much earlier and even those who died outside of the Srebrenica area in 1992 and 1993. This is what I'm talking about. I am trying to present to the Court what the basis is of such conclusions that I'm drawing as forensic expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let me tell you what Professor Wright had to say about the different levels of putrefaction that you say can only indicate that the bodies were deposited there at separate times. At transcript 22307 - and this is when you were in the courtroom - he said: "There was certainly differences in the stage of decomposition of the bodies and that depended on where they were, where an individual lay in the mass of bodies. If you're buried in a mass grave on the very edge of the bodies, then you putrefy much faster and you're reduced to a skeletal stage much faster than the individuals in the middle of the mass of bodies. So they're not all at the same stage of decomposition, but the differences in the stages of decomposition can be interpreted in terms of where the body lies in the body mass when executed." So do you accept that different rates of decomposition doesn't necessarily mean they were buried at different times; it can actually be a result of where the body is in the mass grave, can't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me three seconds to find something. Precisely that which Professor Lawrence said had to do with putrefaction in the mass grave and the location of the body within the mass grave and that it had a bearing on stages in decomposition and that is correct. However, what you went on to read further, that it depended on where the body was shot dead, is not correct, because not all the bodies in the grave were shot dead, not all of them were executed. That's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, I didn't -- no, no, stop there --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- true and I do not accept that. Now, the third thing which is important which I'm trying to locate --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I didn't say anything about where the bodies were shot dead. I'm purely saying, as Professor Wright said, the location of the body within the grave can affect the rate of decomposition, can't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is all right, but you went on to read something else. Can you read for me what it was in the transcript of Professor Lawrence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I don't know what you are asking, Professor. I didn't say anything about where the bodies were shot, but I can tell you what Professor Lawrence said or Dr. Lawrence said on this point at transcript 22482, again when you were here. He said: "There is often a great deal of variation in how fast a body can decompose. In addition, work done on mass graves from the Second World War demonstrates that. On the outside of the grave, the bodies decompose faster than on the inside of the grave simply because of proximity to air, to water, and that in the centre of the grave one tends to see less decomposition because there is less oxygen, so a degree of variation is not at all uncommon in a mass grave." Let me ask you again, Professor, do you agree that different rates of decomposition can be explained by different conditions within a single grave?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. However, during this court proceeding that I attended, Professor Lawrence also said this: Variation in putrefaction also indicates different times of death and different times of interment. Now, in answer to this question put by Mr. Karadzic, he answered yes, and this is what I'm claiming for the Chamber. It is not just the pit itself and the position of bodies in that mass grave that have a bearing, but also different times of death and different times of interment. You have to mind this. When we're talking about different times of death, this is something that we continue to disregard. The time of death does not have to coincide with the time of interment. That's quite clear. Death could have happened several months back and then the body may have been buried with others. And if it died several months earlier, then you have decomposition, skeletonisation, mummification, and saponification, and then if you take this body and bury it together with three or four others in a single grave, this time of death will not coincide with those other times of death. That's what I'm saying. Now, I suggested that Mr. Karadzic put that question to him at the time and his answer was given on the 8th of December, 2012. That was when I was listening to it. So I do accept this part of what he said, what had a bearing on putrefaction, but do allow me to say this other bit because it is, after all, part of my expertise. I'm not talking about other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Well, if you accept the evidence of the exhumation leaders that each of these graves was a single interment, that the bodies were put there all at one time, just accept the truth of that for a moment, Professor, if that's the case, the reason why you see different rates of decomposition in the grave is purely down to the different conditions within the grave, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. And the question? I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you again. Just accept the evidence of the exhumation leaders that each of these graves was a single deposit. Just accept the truth of that for a moment. If that's the case, the different rates of decomposition within that grave can be explained purely by the fact that it's a mass grave and there are different conditions within that grave; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a phenomenal construction of a question. If I say "yes," then I confirm the thesis. I will say "yes," however, with a caveat. The different degree of putrefaction in one grave where there was a simultaneous interment does not have to be only a reflection of conditions in that grave but also a reflection of the time of death, the way people died, and the conditions that the body was surrounded with before burial. With that caveat that Lawrence also agreed with, I will say yes. I will say that one of the conditions of the degree of putrefaction and the appearance of the bodies in the grave is the condition of the grave and the place where the body is found in the grave. Fine. Okay. I agree, but with the caveat that I've just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let's move to a different topic now, your theory about the DNA connections between the primary and the secondary graves. Now, you testified at transcript 41751 that if a body part in a secondary grave doesn't have a DNA connection to a primary grave, then that secondary grave is actually the primary grave for that body part. Have I understood that correctly?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. And you say at various parts --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. It represents perhaps a primary grave for those bodies which do not have a DNA connection with another primary grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we see, for example, in your most recent report, your August 2012 report, that - this is at page 18 and the 65 ter number is 1D25488 - you say that: "Other bodies from these graves which were not connected by DNA to other bodies were actually buried there primarily. In other words, there is no evidence, no evidence, that the other bodies were moved." Is that -- that's your evidence as you sit here, there is no evidence --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the gist of my evidence and I will gladly repeat this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. So you weren't aware then when you wrote this opinion that it's an adjudicated fact in this case that there are ballistic, soil, and other material links between those mass graves, between the primary and secondary mass graves?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean what was said in the Vujadin Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, no. I'm just asking you, you say that unless there's a DNA connection, there is no evidence that the other bodies were moved. And I'm asking you whether you were aware that there are links between the graves established by ballistics, by soil, and by material --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of that. I was aware of all the ballistic findings and the artefacts, and I knew that the connection was established between primary and secondary graves. This is correct. There are connections between primary and secondary graves. However, I said that in those secondary graves where there were connections with primary graves, a DNA connection speaks of biological material and that biological material can be connected to just one person for whom a DNA was established. Not all the other bodies - and there were hundreds of them - were connected to a primary grave. This is what I was saying. So if we have ten connections here between a secondary and a primary grave or a primary and another primary grave, you can ask me why that would be the case because a body may be split. However, the other bodies or the other body parts that are found in that secondary grave do not have to originate from the primary grave, irrespective of the projectiles that may have been found there. This is what I'm saying and this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, you'd agree that one reason why there mightn't be a DNA connection between a primary and a secondary grave for a particular body is because that body was dug up in its entirety from the primary grave and moved in its entirety to the secondary grave? You'd agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. This is one of the possibilities, a possibility of that kind exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, we've seen in your report, Professor, you cite to some witness statements. You have the witness statement of the commander of the road platoon from the Zvornik Brigade, Damjan Lazarevic, who was not only at Orahovac, Kozluk, and Branjevo Farm during the initial burials; he was also there while those graves were dug up to be reburied. Did you have that statement?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. I don't have that. I didn't use that, no, no. I don't know what you're talking about, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. So you didn't have any witness statements which actually described the primary graves being dug up and the contents moved to the secondary graves?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No. The only statements that I had in the Vujadin Popovic case are the statements of the witnesses whose ERN numbers I have provided. They describe the way how they tried to break through from Srebrenica into the surrounding forests. As an expert, said that it was not up to me to be the judge of their testimonies; it was up to the Trial Chamber to do that. And I only used the segment from their statement that indicated the way they were killed, what types of fire-arms were used in those incidents, and what was important was that we established that around Srebrenica during that period of time, between the 11th and the 19th of July, when they embarked on that breakthrough to the free territory outside of Srebrenica, they came across a lot of bodies which were in the various stages of putrefaction. Alic Hasan is a witness whose testimony I quote from, confirm that, and I found that very important. The witness who testified here under an ERN number, he said that he came across a group of a hundred killed people from Srebrenica, and another witness stated that due to the shelling and artillery weapons fire, one of their columns, that number between 3- and 4.000 people who were withdrawing through the forest came under attack. Look here, 3- to 4.000 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let me -- let me stop you there --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- of people were crossing through the woods and they were attacked --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: We --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- hold on, hold on, let me -- let me finish. I have only these witnesses, nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have that other witness whom you have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. So when in your August 2012 report you said other than DNA connections there is no evidence that the other bodies were moved, you weren't taking account of witness statements, ballistic evidence, soil evidence, or material evidence, were you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So, sorry, "yes," you weren't taking account of those things?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can we go to 65 ter 25488, page 21 in the English and 18 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: This is your August 2012 report, Professor. You'll see conclusion (d) or point (d), you say: "The analysis" conducted to date "of the mechanism of injury and the manner of injury in the cases I have analysed so far ... points to the fact that in the majority of cases the injuries could have occurred in combat, i.e., armed conflict, either by fire-arms, shells, or explosives, and that all the exhumed bodies do not have the characteristics of an 'execution' ('death by shooting') ..." So that's your opinion, that all of the bodies exhumed lack the characteristics of an execution by firing squad?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we talking about the chapter entitled the way deaths were caused or the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: It's down the bottom of the page, sub-point (d). It's on the screen in front of you --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- down the bottom of the page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes. Now I can see it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you the question again. It's your opinion that all of the bodies exhumed lacked the characteristics of an execution by firing squad?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you read this carefully - I'm talking about exhibit (d) - I said and I underline, the injuries inflicted by fire-arms, I'm trying to rephrase now, do not show proof that they were inflicted by execution. If you -- when you say "execution," you mean death by shooting, these wounds do not have those characteristics. I wanted to emphasise that the opinion that was given and that was that those were injuries inflicted by execution and this is what Haglund describes as additional wounds from bullets on the heads of several victims point to the fact that fire was opened from close range, I do not agree with that opinion provided by Mr. Haglund. And let me say why. If a body is putrefied or skeletised and the bodies were in that condition, because that's how they were described, and if there are ten wounds on that body, I as a forensic expert, I don't know whether the wound in the occipital part of the head was the first that was inflicted and it was followed by others or the other way around. I cannot determine the sequence of the wounding. This is not what we can do in our profession. I cannot accept this. I can only say that there is a wound on the head, but I can't say whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- it was inflicted by execution, i.e., whether the pistol barrel was on the head of the victim. I can't even see the gunpowder traces. This is what I'm talking about. This means that a majority of the bodies which were injured from fire-arms do show characteristics of having been wounded in a war conflict. Some of them even show elements that may be accepted as being inflicted as a result of execution, and those were all those people who had ligatures on their bodies. And as a forensics expert, I may be in a position to conclude that they were executed. So this is the explanation of what I wrote in my report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gunpowder traces, the Professor said "at the point of impact around the wound," this is what the Professor said and this is missing from line 21. [In English] "I can't even see the gunpowder traces ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, Professor, you've been critical of Dr. John Clark in particular for allegedly stating that for the vast majority death cannot be linked to conflict. And if we go back to page 11 in the English and page 10 in the B/C/S of this report, and you'll see in the first paragraph under point 4, manner of injury, you say: "John Clark's position (presented in his report ERN 0308 0711 ... is that," and you include this in inverted commas, "'for the vast majority, death cannot be linked to combat ...'" Professor, just have a look at, in your report, the phrase that you've got in inverted commas in the B/C/S and then we'll take a quick look at Dr. Clark's report and see if that phrase actually exists. You can see that sentence there in inverted commas. "'For the vast majority, death cannot be linked to combat ...'" It's on the next page in the B/C/S. Professor, you can --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- see that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, if we can have Exhibit P105 [sic] in e-court, page 28 in the English and 32 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's Exhibit P4105, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you can see here, Professor, there's absolutely nothing in here that says "for the vast majority, death cannot be linked to combat." If we zoom out the B/C/S a little bit, this is the exact page you were referring to in your report, isn't it, 0308-0711?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, this is the report; however, this you will find at the beginning and I kept on repeating that thing in my report. This is a quote from that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, Professor, you've specifically given --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- this ERN and the words that you have quoted from the translation in your report don't actually appear in Dr. Clark's report or anything remotely like it. The point I'm making, Professor, is you've quoted language from Dr. Clark's report or supposedly quoted language that isn't actually there so you could set up an argument so you could critique it; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Perhaps we could take the break and --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, I -- yes, give me a break. I'll then look at all the documents because this is a direct quote from his report. Perhaps the page indication is wrong, but this was quoted from his aggregate reports dealing with all these three locations, the aggregate report this thick.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, Professor, it can't be just a number -- an ERN mistake because you actually quote. You say it's from the page that contains the overall conclusions from the three grave-sites. So it's not just a numerical error; you're obviously talking about this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. -- just a second. Professor Dunjic, do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we come back to this after the break so that the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- Professor could have a moment to take a look into the entire report. And shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'm about to move to something slightly different, Mr. President, so now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So if it is convenient --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- would be a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- shall we take a break. Yes, we'll break until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Professor be provided with the entire report from which the quote originates? Can he be provided the report in hard copy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, I'll find it. I'll find it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have not more than 33 pages. This is all I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that the Professor has everything -- all the documents. If necessary, through the Victims and Witnesses Section, he can ask for further material, either to the Prosecution or the Defence. 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Professor, did you have an opportunity to take a look at the reports referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did, I did. And I have to apologise right away to say that Mr. Mitchell is right when he quoted this page or when he cited this page. That is the original, the document, that I mentioned as a number. However, the whole report is 30-odd pages in which Mr. Clark explained what he found in these three locations. And as for what I wrote, that in that document, thinking of the whole document, not just the overall conclusions, it says for a large majority death cannot be linked to combat. And I found in his statement of the 20th of February, 2007, in the Vujadin Popovic case where he said in relation to these three locations, he drew a conclusion that for a majority of the cases death cannot be linked to combat. So from his overall conclusion, it arises that these people in these three locations, Ravnice, Glogova, and Zeleni Jadar, were found with gun-shot wounds of different calibres, and none of the men in these graves carried any weaponry or military uniforms. In answer to the question whether these are fighters or not, then on the 20th of February he said that a large majority of deaths cannot be linked to combat, so I found that in the main report for the Karadzic case on page 52. Therefore, that sentence is part of his overall conclusions for these three locations. Then I, in relation to that assertion and in relation to information as an expert when I inspected the locations and these other documents, wrote that that assertion, that it cannot be accepted that a large majority cannot be linked to combat, said it could not be accepted and I explained why I wrote that. And you are right, Mr. Mitchell, to the extent that that is that page 711, that's the last page here, the overall conclusions, and I looked at his whole report which has over 30 pages, where, among other things, he said later at the trial -- he stated this sentence, so that I made an error that was not deliberate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Just one more question on this particular thing, Professor. We've reviewed Dr. Clark's report from cover to cover, and I believe it's correct to say it doesn't actually mention the word "combat" once in this whole report. It's not just this page.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Combat is not mentioned. That is a term that I used. I'm talking about armed conflict, or rather, when I say "armed conflict," "oruzani sukob," I mean those woundings and injuries by various instruments, especially when we're talking about shrapnel. Shrapnel is not used for executions or death by firing. Therefore, I say that this was in combat or was not in combat or was in a war conflict or not in a war conflict. So this is where I make my difference so that it would not be interpreted wrongly. I said very precisely that for those cases where it was established beyond doubt that they were tied, that they had ligatures and so on and so forth, for those 450 to 500 people for whom it was established that beyond doubt, I state as a forensics expert that it was an execution regardless of the injuries inflicted, or rather, what they were like by localisation, number, and so on and so forth. But as a forensics man, I still claim that other injuries that were noted that were caused by shrapnel, by shells, cannot be connected to executions. And this is where I make my significant difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Professor, as you know, our time is a bit limited, so if you could keep your answer simple and short. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, let's go back to your substantive criticism that all the bodies exhumed lack the characteristics of an execution by firing squad. And what I'd like to do now is go through two scenarios in this case, one is an execution by firing squad and one is an execution that involved the use of grenades, and get your views on whether what you saw in the autopsy reports are consistent with that evidence. The first scenario is based on the evidence we have for the Branjevo Farm execution, and you reviewed some of the autopsy reports from the Pilica site, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can have in e-court 1D07723.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: This is the witness statement of Franc Kos who was a member of the 10th Sabotage Detachment who was at the Branjevo Farm on the 16th of July, 1995, and who was convicted in the State Court for participating in the killings there. What Mr. Kos says in this statement is: "They unloaded 25 people," he's talking about the Branjevo Farm, "half the bus. I say '25 people,' there may have been fewer. They took them to the field in one group where Zoran Goronja was standing behind the M84, who I had assigned as security. Marko Boskic was standing next to him and then Marko Boskic told him, 'Step on it, kid. What are you waiting for?' And then Zoran Goronja started shooting. He fired 10 or 20 rounds maybe, but since he was small and light, the M84 knocked him over." And then Mr. Kos goes on to say that a number of soldiers stepped-up and fired volleys from their automatic rifles and they did the same thing with the second group. And there were many wounded, so he went and put them out of their misery and shot four of them in the head. So what Franc Kos is describing in his statement is an execution, it's not armed conflict, is it, Professor?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And he described shots to the head, shots to the body, the use of an M84 machine-gun, and the use of automatic rifles. Now, all of that is consistent with the evidence that you saw in the autopsy reports for the Pilica site; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Right. Well, Mr. Karadzic is calling Franc Kos as a witness in his defence next week to give this evidence about the Branjevo Farm executions. Professor, did they tell you -- did the Defence tell you before you testified, before they asked you to take the stand and say that this was armed conflict, that they were going to be calling evidence that this was an execution a week after you testified?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the reference. Where did we say that these people who died in the Branjevo Farm died in combat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Robinson, did the Defence ever confirm they were executed in Branjevo Farm?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, we haven't taken -- we haven't taken any position on that by any evidence so far that we've led.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we continue, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: My question, Professor, was: Were you told that the Defence was calling Franc Kos as a witness to describe the Branjevo Farm executions?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let me just put two more pieces of information to you. This is the evidence of Drazen Erdemovic now, which is Exhibit P332 in this case. And at transcript page 10971 in that exhibit, Mr. Erdemovic said: "The first people from that bus were blindfolded and their hands were tied behind their backs." That's consistent with the evidence that you saw in the Pilica autopsy reports, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And Erdemovic also said that: "We were ordered to shoot at them. They had their backs to us." Now, evidence of shots to the back of the victims is also consistent with the autopsy reports you reviewed, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Professor, there were --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to be precise, in those cases where the entry wounds and injuries were noted on the back of the body, from the head to the trunk and the extremities, that is consistent in that part. You understand? That is consistent with the testimony of this witness that you referred to. I don't know what he said, that they were turned -- that their backs were turned. So in that sense, I believe that is consistent with those autopsy reports where the wounds or injuries were found on the back of the corpses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: There were 132 individuals exhumed from the Pilica Branjevo Farm grave; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot check that now. I assume that that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, you can take my word that that's what it says in Dr. Haglund's report, which is Exhibit P4321. And Dr. Haglund -- Dr. Haglund's report also says that 77 of those individuals had their wrists bound and there were ligatures associated with a further five victims. And your evidence in the Popovic case was that you didn't look at the autopsy reports for the victims with ligatures; you only looked at the ones without ligatures. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was when I testified?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just asking you to confirm that you only looked at the autopsy reports for bodies that didn't have a ligature because you accepted that the ones with ligatures were executed?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accepted that those with ligatures were executed. Just one moment. You said how many? 100? 130 -- Pilica ... Yes, I have a list here from 2007. I cannot find -- ah, Pilica, a large number of autopsies but there is no precise number. This is your document --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Right. The --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- where it's listed by locations, but I did process Pilica --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- those who did not have ligatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, that was the point I was getting at. You looked at the autopsy reports for bodies without ligatures?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you accepted that the bodies which did have ligatures were executed?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, Professor, when forming your view that all of the bodies exhumed lacked the characteristics of an execution by firing squad, wouldn't it have been helpful for you to compare the injuries on the bodies with ligatures who you accepted were executed with the bodies without ligatures and see if there was any consistency between the injuries on those two sets of bodies?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not do that. I accepted immediately that the bodies with ligatures were executed. For the bodies for which there were no ligatures on the arms and legs, the injuries that were observed were not injuries which could be with certainty said to be caused by execution.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to repeat the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Professor, Professor, probably you were speaking a bit too fast. The interpreters were not able to catch the last sentence --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- could you repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those bodies where there were no ligatures on the arms or on any other part of the body for which I said that they were executed and I accept that conclusion, that opinion, that's one thing. All the other bodies where there were no ligatures and if there were injuries I did not make a comparative analysis. Such injuries by fire-arms are seen on people in the case of execution, regardless of whether the front or the back of the body is facing that direction. So by number and the localisation of the entry wounds, these kinds of injuries can also be seen in armed conflict. That is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes. But you'd agree that it would be a useful thing to do to compare the injuries on the group of bodies with ligatures with those without because if those two groups have similar injuries, that would suggest that they were killed in the same way; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a certain way, that could be accepted with certain caveats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Just one more point on this particular scenario. In your big report, the combination of three reports that came from the Popovic case, you make the point that where projectiles are found in a body, that could mean the victim suffered a long-range combat injury because the bullet might have slowed down and lost energy when it hit the victim. Do you recall that -- those parts of your report?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that and I will reply immediately. In a certain number of victims, projectiles were found, as we saw yesterday, in their bodies. Those projectiles, as explained by ballistics and experts who were your experts also, I agree, they have large speed and degree of penetration. So the question is how you can find in one body three projectiles, for example, the projectile shell, parts of the projectile? What does such an autopsy finding indicate? To me as an expert, I as an expert then answer that that would mean that in view of the characteristics of a weapon, it means that either it was fired from a large distance or the projectiles were passing through some kind of obstacles which slowed them down or they passed through some bodies previously and then stopped in the body where the projectile was found. That would mean that. So from the forensic aspect, that projectile with a large degree of penetration and speed in normal circumstances could pass through the body and could cause certain injuries in soft and hard tissue. But I also have to think in the option as to how and from which distance the projectile was fired and did it pass through somebody's body before that or through some other obstacle, meaning that it would be slowed down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, let me --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 2, the Professor said: But if it stays, and that did not --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter did not hear the end of that sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: But if -- [Interpretation] But if it stopped, I also have to think of options.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we continue, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, let me give you or describe to you how the Branjevo Farm executions unfolded that day based on the evidence in this case. There's a group of prisoners taken off a bus and lined up in the field and they're shot, and then a second group is lined up directly behind those dead bodies and they're shot. And this goes on for several hours with each row lined up behind the one before. So as the bullets are passing through those bodies, there are other dead bodies lined up behind them in rows. So isn't another reasonable explanation for bullet fragments in these bodies that the ones on the ground had been hit by bodies [sic] passing through the prisoners who were then being shot at that particular moment? That's a reasonable explanation for why those bodies contain projectiles, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, and I said that. That is one of the explanations that is logical, a logical explanation. When you pass it through a barrier, the barrier could be a body, a tree, a slab. So I put all of these questions and this is something that applies to this one locality where there are witness statements which would be consistent with the ligatures as well. And so I'm not denying any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move to the second scenario, which is an execution involving grenades. And we see in your August 2012 report at page 13, that's 65 ter 25488, and you're describing the injuries on the bodies from the Ravnice, Glogova, and Zeleni Jadar 5 graves, and you say that the blast injuries that are present on some of those bodies are consistent with armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And it's that point in your report where you refer to a number of witness statements that describe armed conflict in the area; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: But you don't cite to a single witness statement that describes the use of grenades at the Kravica warehouse, do you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only had these statements and I cited and quoted those.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me read you something else from Mr. Karadzic's Defence witness Franc Kos. And this is at page 15 of his statement where he says: "Members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment were at the Kravica warehouse," and he says: "Marko Boskic," who is another member of the unit, "headed towards the depot, took two hand-grenades and then threw them into the depot on the right-hand side in which the people who were alive were, two hand-grenades." So Mr. Karadzic's evidence from one of his witnesses is that grenades were used at the Kravica warehouse. Now, that would assist you in determining why the bodies in graves connected with the Kravica warehouse had blast injuries on them; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, Professor, you've testified in a Srebrenica case at this Tribunal before in the Popovic case, and you know that a significant body of evidence about the executions exists. Did you ask the Defence for any of those witness statements or any of that evidence when you were drafting your reports for this case?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received all the reports that were provided to Mr. Karadzic. I already stated how many of them there were in electronic form. There were files, folders, DVDs, images, et cetera. Everything that I received I -- well, I managed to review a part of it. I did not seek nor did I receive any sort of witness statements that you are now referring to. I adhered to, or rather, I dealt with the forensic aspect of it. In the Vujadin Popovic case, I received documents from the Defence, the witness statements that I quoted where I concluded that people were killed also by explosives. In some of the material related to Kravica, there were elements where the use of explosives was indicative. I'm not denying that. You now told me that a witness said that two hand-grenades were thrown in. Grenades would inflict smaller or larger injuries from shrapnel and they might result in the death of several individuals on whose bodies metal segments can be found. In those bodies where metal segments were found, that's to say shrapnel, for those individuals it could be said that they were killed by this sort of action. However, let me say also this, that in other localities where there is a presence of this occurrence, this does not exclude combat and the fact that deaths were the result of combat. I cannot disregard the evidence of the individuals who testified here who speak to a large number of casualties, the use of mortars, PAMs, and other weapons of high fire-power. Alic Hasan, Mehmet Alic, Enver Abdic, et cetera, they talk about how people who were around them were killed. I want to say that there is evidence of the use of very destructive weapons, shells, mortar shells, PAMs, projectiles of high calibre, et cetera. On the basis of this, I draw a conclusion that a large number of people were killed in some sort of armed conflict and nothing more than that. I am not denying it. I am only confirming.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, Professor, you just said: I cannot disregard the evidence of those individuals who talked about armed conflict. You did disregard all of the evidence about the executions, didn't you? The Defence didn't provide it to you and you didn't ask for it, despite seeing some of that evidence when you testified here in 2008 in the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I testified in the Popovic case and I explained and examined all these cases; however, I did not have the statements of the witnesses that you just put to me nor were these statements given to me by the Defence.
