However, even what you have just told me will not in substance change the main conclusion that arises from my expertise. So let's say I will accept that 500 people were executed, but also that many people in the area were killed in combat. I have to also emphasise, because of the sake of the Tribunal and the truth, that a great many of individuals who went missing and who are linked with the events in Srebrenica between 11 and 19 July 1995 were buried in these primary or secondary graves, but that they were brought over there at a later stage or that their deaths date far earlier than the events in Srebrenica. So there are three groups of victims there, and I have to make this clear to the Tribunal because the documents that I analysed confirm it. You asked me a moment ago about Bratunac, about the 80 victims that Mr. Pejakovic in that school -- that Mr. Pejakovic found and said should be buried. That was 1992. And they are included on the list of the Srebrenica victims. I don't see what sort of connection or link --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, you have just --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- there should be and this is what I'm talking about --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You have just completely made that up. Mr. Pejakovic went to Bratunac, looked at a hundred bodies, and said: Bury them in a grave. You have no idea who those people are, so how could you know that they're on the Srebrenica missing list? You don't know who those hundred people in 1992 were, do you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wait a minute, let's not talk this way. I'm not here to invent things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, you just said -- Professor, you just said that those hundred people from Bratunac are on the Srebrenica missing list. You don't know who those hundred people from Bratunac are, do you, that Dr. Pejakovic or Professor Pejakovic went and looked at in 1992 and said: Put them in a mass grave? You have no idea who those people are, do you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will prove it to you that I am not making it up. I know about these individuals and I know what Professor Pejakovic did. However, in the corrigendum by Dusan Janc - why do I keep going back to him? - says that in Bratunac -- so bodies of other persons from -- other than those from Kravica were brought to the Glogova grave and he says --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yet -- that's --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- where from, including Bratunac up to 80 individuals. So I am --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- referring and relying on this document. It wasn't in 1992, but these people were killed in Bratunac in 1992. When was it --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in 1992 that those people in Bratunac were killed --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I don't know if you're deliberately conflating these two. Professor Pejakovic looked at a hundred bodies in the school in Bratunac in 1992. Dusan Janc is talking about 80 bodies from the Vuk Karadzic school in 1995. They are completely separate things, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not -- he's not speaking about 1995. Dusan Janc speaks about Bratunac, 80 bodies, and around the school. So these locations include the area in and around school Vuk Karadzic in Bratunac, up to 80 bodies, and this is written in the corrigendum by Dusan Janc. I'm not inventing anything nor am I compiling things or collating them --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- this is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- your expert opinion is that Dusan Janc is talking about the same bodies that Professor Pejakovic looked at in 1992 and said: Put them in a mass grave? That's your expert testimony, that those two are the same event?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my expertise. Professor Pejakovic looked and examined between 80 and 100 bodies in that school. He said that they should be buried because of the risk of an epidemics. Where did those bodies come from? Where they were buried? Where they were taken to? I don't know nor does anybody present here know that. However, we have the report. When I looked at Mr. Janc's report, I tied Bratunac and the school in with this where they were probably buried, around the school, and these are the bodies that he is referring to in connection with the correction of the list of Srebrenica victims, no more. I don't know their names. I don't know their exact number. So I am not speculating at all. I'm merely drawing upon this document and the knowledge that I gained, and unfortunately so, back there at the time, or rather, based on what I heard from Professor Pejakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So a hundred nameless bodies buried in 1992 are on the Srebrenica missing list, even though you have no idea who they are?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Just as Potocari 1 and Potocari 2 had those buried in them from 1993. Tisova Kosa 1, and I wrote all of this in my report. People who are precisely known to have died at such and such a time and where. Even the BH army says that there were people who were killed in connection with Srebrenica in combat in 1993, 1994 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, just stick to the question --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- all the way through to May of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: The question was, you made an assertion that those hundred bodies that Professor Pejakovic saw in the school in Bratunac are on the Srebrenica missing list. You have no idea who those hundred Muslims that Professor Pejakovic saw were? You don't know their identities, do you? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have any further questions. I'm not going to address the ABiH list with Dr. Dunjic. It's a demographics issue. Dr. Tabeau's report specifically deals with this issue, that's P4995, pages 93 to 98, that's our evidence and we rely on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellencies. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me start from the last issue, Professor. You were asked if you had read all the witness statements. What was the main bulk of material that you examined?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main material was pathologists' reports and autopsy reports. In addition to documents that may be used to estimate the time of death, mechanism of injury, and circumstances prevailing in 1995 and after July 1995. So these were the documents presented to me, exhumations, method of work, method of exhumation, method of autopsy, et cetera. Now, reports relating to certain locations by pathologists, anthropologists, or archaeologists were the basis for the examination of individual autopsy reports. As an expert, my duty was not just toward you but toward the Trial Chamber, the Defence, and the Prosecution to point to certain illogicalities or to certain things that were not in line with the medical profession, to point to possible deficiencies or shortcomings, and to establish that the number of victims related to the Srebrenica events of July -- or rather, to establish what the number is and whether it is linked to executions only or to some other mechanism of injury at some other time or in some other place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 42 of today's transcript, Mr. Mitchell described how the executions at Branjevo took place according to a witness statement. It was said that the next line would stand behind those who were executed. So if they stand behind them, how is it possible for the bullets intended for them to end up in the bodies of those who are in front of them?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I understand you correctly. From what I understood, the Prosecutor said that they were standing in front of those who had already been executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, the other way around. At page 42, Mr. Mitchell said that the disposition was exactly the other way around, that the first line would be executed and that then behind that line the next row of people would be executed. Under such circumstances, was it possible for the bullets to kill that group of people and at the same time end up in the bodies of those who had already been executed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, where did Mr. Mitchell say that the second line was lined up behind or before the first line? Are you referring to page 42, line --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, line 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All he said: And then a second group is lined up behind those dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly, behind the dead bodies and not in front of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Perhaps it's -- my language wasn't precise enough, Mr. President. I think it's clear when I say: "As the bullets are passing through those bodies, there are other dead bodies lined up behind them in rows." That's the scenario.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was my understanding of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, Mr. Mitchell relied on the testimony of a witness who said that they would have been lined up behind and not in front --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, with respect, I think you are confused about this. I mean, nobody would suggest that -- the bullets may go through a front row and into the back row, but nobody's going to suggest that they go through the front row into the back row and then back into the front row. It's just a matter of common sense.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On several occasions in the course of today's session, for example, at page 28 and later, you were told that this was some connection with Janc's report, that there were no indications of executions. This is what was held against you when you said it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have P04505, page 83. Let's see what Investigator Manning had to say about this. No, the number isn't correct. I said P04505. 4505. I apologise. There is a mistake that I made. It's not the report. It's a different number. It's 4502 it seems. 4504. Apologies. Can we have page 83 in Serbian. It's 59, the pagination of the document, but the page in e-court is 83. We have the right page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor, please, have a look at the 47 relatively intact bodies. In respect of which of these bodies can one claim that they were executed ?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the English version for the parties? It may be page 59. There it is. Can we have the Serbian version back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could just confirm, I believe we're talking about -- this is about Zeleni Jadar 5, but if Mr. Karadzic could just confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if we look at the previous pages we will see exactly which one it is. I wasn't much dealing with that. I wanted to take one page as an example. It deals with 47 relatively intact bodies. Zeleni Jadar 5.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see it down there. Can you repeat the question now? I'm trying to read everything that is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the top. 33 had a cause of death as gun-shot wounds, one gun-shot and shrapnel wounds. Under 2, two had probable gun-shot wounds. Three had possible gun-shot wounds, one possible as gun-shot and shrapnel. And for 9 undetermined, and of these, seven had small metal fragments present. For which of these bodies can one claim in front of the Tribunal that they were executed by firing squad?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to answer your question, as a professional, I would have to have a look at the autopsy report for Zeleni Jadar 5 and state for those who have gun-shot injuries and who had ligatures that they were executed by firing squad, as I did previously. However, there is no ligature for the 33 persons who were established to have died as a result of gun-shot injuries. This is something that can possibly be said but not claimed with certainty. This is not the sort of injury that would militate in favour of either of these two options in my view. However, the conclusions drawn here as to the cause of death are quite interesting and I think quite proper. On the one hand, we are given degrees of probability as to WHAT the cause of death which is much more important than the actual cause of death. In one or two, cause of death was established; and two or three, there was a probability, possibly yes or no gun-shot injury; and under three, the injuries could possibly be linked with possible cause of death. So definitely in those cases where you cannot conclude that death was the result of gun-shot injuries, for those definitely you could not say that they were executed by firing squad, and this is what one could conclude on the basis of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if there were one-body graves and what did they contain? Multiple-body graves? How did the Muslim side classify grave-sites?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer the question as to how those graves were classified. There were mass graves containing multiple bodies. There were smaller graves with fewer people who were buried there, 10, 20 of them, and we also have one-body graves. The bodies were both brought from the surface where they had been killed, either in a forest or in a field, and in some reports that I perused previously, I saw that there were also individual interments when people were individually buried. But that was more in Central Bosnia and in Eastern Bosnia than elsewhere. I can't remember where exactly in Central Bosnia and so on and so forth. I'm familiar with those types of graves, but they were very few and far between. And that was at the beginning of 1995 and in 1996 in the presence of the prosecutor's office of the Federation and the witnesses who pointed to certain graves and told them: This is where we buried so and so. That's how they completed identifications. And then it turned out that some groups of people who were exhumed were erroneously identified and I wouldn't speculate about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, on page 21 and on page 22 earlier today, we heard allegations who quoted -- where the Prosecutor quoted his expert that the degree of degradation of the bodies in the mass graves depended on the microclimate in the grave and also that the skeletonisation is more probable on the periphery of a grave than in its centre. Can you tell us whether their findings confirm that in the peripheral parts of the grave the bodies are more skeletised than elsewhere? Did their findings show that there is a very clear geographical border, i.e., in one angle the bodies are skeletised and in the other corner of the mass grave the bodies are saponified?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was asserted and what was said, I agreed with the fact that the microclimate in a large grave, in a large pit, differs from one corner to the next and it depends on the thickness of the pile of bodies. And that the bodies that are on the periphery or closer to the surface have undergone a different degree of putrefaction. This is one theoretical aspect. What was very important here was the fact that in those big graves one had to try and analyse post-mortem reports in order to identify putrefaction on certain bodies, in order to compare that putrefaction with the places where the bodies were located in such a grave. This is the beginning of my answer. I didn't finish. I apologise. I'll try and be very concise from now on. This means that in post-mortem reports - and I'm trying to be very objective here - post-mortem reports were very superficial in terms of the description of putrefaction. This was all very generalised and very imprecise. I trust Lawrence and Clark. I know that they are forensic experts. They know how bodies change in a grave. However, in the post-mortem reports that were part of the overall report, I couldn't find the putrefaction described in a proper way, in a very concise way. The pathologist who performed post-mortems varied in the way it described bodies. Even Lawrence and Clark said at one point that the putrefaction was not sufficiently described, and they tried to describe why there is a difference. I started from that, and in the analysis of the putrefaction and the decomposition of the bodies, I arrived at a conclusion that putrefaction was not only subject to the difference in the conditions in the graveyard but also the time of death and the time of interment and this is a very important conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I go back to one point. If we accept the theory according to which microclimate is decisive, has it been established that certain parts of the grave led to skeletonisation without any discrimination of all the bodies? In other words, were those bodies mixed or were they separate and were they consistent with microclimate in different parts of the graveyard? Did they provide proof that all the bodies on one side were skeletised?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My shortest answer would be: No, there was no such proof. There was no evidence to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some general assertions to the effect that most of the bodies were skeletised, that some of them were saponified, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that on the periphery of the graveyards there were saponified bodies, whereas there were some skeletised bodies in the centre? Were there bodies adjacent to each other exposed to the same microclimate of which one was saponified and the other skeletised?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such cases. There were differences between a certain number of skeletised and a certain number of saponified bodies with several -- displaying several degrees of saponification, and I said that if such bodies were found in a very consistent microclimate such as a graveyard, then we have to take into consideration the different times of death and the different time of interment. However, the different time of death is perhaps better than the different time of interment because they could have all been buried on the same day but they could already display different degrees of putrefaction. Mr. Christopher Hamilton Lawrence agreed with that when I asked him the same question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 16 and on, it was stated that there was no subsequent interment and the Prosecution relied on its expert here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at D1975 which is Mr. Janc's corrigendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the document to be displayed, they showed you bullet point 2, and you also heard a witness statement according to which in Glogova 1 they were all buried between the 14th and the 17th of July. You will find this on page 16, I suppose, or thereabouts. Please look at the first bullet point. Let's not skip the first bullet point. If all the interments were completed on the 17th of July, how come that the persons who were in Yugoslavia until the 26th of July and they were still found in that grave?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My shortest answer would be that this is proof that there were subsequent burials in that grave, and this is just one piece of evidence testifying to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 4 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps I can be -- clarify this. Grave L at Glogova, Professor Wright testified about that, it was specifically excluded from this case. It's very clear that that's a separate deposit on the side of the grave and that's not part of this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could give the reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'll look --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- for that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, shall we continue, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we also be provided citation whether that was a one-off, 12 were buried, 10 were from Serbia, and they were all buried on different dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 4 earlier today, it was suggested to you that it is up to the Trial Chamber to decide how things transpired, whether they transpired in one way or another. And according to you, is the Trial Chamber entitled to hear a second opinion which contests the first opinion?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not a question for me, as a matter of fact, but what I am duty-bound to say and as an expert is my opinion. I have to share with all of you what I have noted that may be of some assistance to clarify the events and the developments, and I have to tell you whether something may or may not be accepted from the professional standpoint and how things can be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We're waiting for a document. And now I would like to go back to what was discussed yesterday on page 100, and that was the destruction of artefacts.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Artefacts, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. Did you do it intentionally? Were you forced to do it because of something?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand. Did I do it intentionally?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now we're talking about Racak, we are talking about those samples that deteriorated.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. Hold on. I didn't answer. Something's going on when we're talking about those samples that we took from Racak for DNA analysis that Mr. Mitchell asked me about. Those samples were taken to the forensic institute -- actually, we're talking about Radonjic Lake, not about Racak. Those samples taken from the bones and the tissues they were taken, I was in charge of the whole procedure, they were taken to the Forensic Medicine Institute and they were placed in the freezer and that was in 1998. In the meantime, when the bombing took place in 1999, the notorious bombing, and when there were outages of electricity, that freezer did not have the supply of electricity. There was no additional cooling energy. And then in 2000 or 2001, that is, three and a half years later, the samples were supposed to be taken out. They were in nylon bags with markings, some of the markings were within the bags, some of them were on the bags, and that's why the samples were mixed, some of the markings had been lost, and they had deteriorated in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to finish before the break. So this was not done intentionally?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 89 you were asked about the difference in the treatment of civilian clothes found on the casualties in Kosovo and those in Bosnia. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what were the formations on the Serbian side that were engaged in Kosovo, were they civilians or who were they? What could have been the casualty as a result of fighting as opposed to the casualty as a result of execution?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you have forced me to try and remember things as they happened in 1998. In Kosovo we had the KLA as a terrorist organisation that was terrorising both Albanians and Serbians, Albanians who didn't want to join them, they were Albanians. And on the other side we had the so-called legal subjectivity and the territory was defended by the army and the police. On the one side we had people in uniform and on the other side we had KLA members who did not sport any specific uniforms before -- I don't know what year. However, they were all in civilian clothes. Some did have military uniforms, but their uniforms were not complete. And they also had special units, i.e., they had the police of which we learned at the time that they wore black jeans and black leather jackets. This is the information that I received and now I'm sharing it with you. They mostly wore civilian clothes. Later on they were provided with their uniforms with some insignia and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In other words, if you found a Serb casualty in Kosovo not wearing a uniform, would that allow you to conclude that that person was a civilian, unlike in Bosnia where a Bosnian war was waged by civilians?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is beyond the scope of my professional expertise; however, among the casualties in Kosovo there were mostly Serbs, civilians, peasants, elderly women, and obviously middle-aged males. But they were all civilians wearing civilian clothes. And it is a well-known fact that they were killed because of their ethnic affiliation. Among them, there were a lot of Albanians who were killed because they didn't want to help the KLA and the third group were Albanians who were of a different religion. They were also killed. And as far as the second segment goes, I wrote that in my report and I also stated it. As far as I know, from newspapers and from very documents in Bosnia, the conflict involved the Army of Republika Srpska on the one side and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the other side. At first, the BiH army involved people who did not have military uniforms. They were members of the Territorial Defence, home guards, or whatever they were called. I'm sure that you know it better than I do, but this is what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement that is 5 -- 25380 relating to Kosovo, you found some victims who were women. Would that provide a basis to conclude that these were civilians?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those specific cases I can say absolutely. First of all, these were three or four women, two women were over 75 years old, they were sisters. There was one younger woman - who was killed together with her husband - who had just given birth, but they managed to hide the child. They were killed and burned in a vehicle and thrown into the Radonjic -- into a channel or canal of the Radonjic Lake. And the fourth woman was found later, together with her husband. They were killed because they allegedly came from abroad and did not want to help the KLA because they all had to finance the KLA at that time. That is for those four persons, women, that I recall. And they were all wearing civilian clothing. And for them I can absolutely claim that they were total civilians and innocent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement 25381, you established that the victims in Racak under their civilian clothing wore military underwear, all the same, and boots which were issued by the military. So they come from the military arsenal, are part of military equipment?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that and I testified to that here. Those long johns are long male underwear, grey, which is worn in the army; and the boots also were specific, they had specific markings indicating that this would be an army batch or contingent. And what I recall and from what I can remember now, these were already markings of a company, or rather, a dispatch or delivery from some firm that uses the letter O with two dots above it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender these two statements by Professor Dunjic that were also used by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I think what is more important than the clothing is the fact that the traces of a gunpowder explosion were found on the palms or hands of those victims from Racak and they also had injuries that are characteristic for fire-arm wounds when a person is semi-bent behind some kind of shelter or shield or cover. And this is something that I said to the Prosecution and this is also something that was established by the Finnish team headed by a professor who was heading the team and then the -- also another member of the team was Helena Ranta.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the name of the first Finnish person who led the team. And could Mr. Karadzic please repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said yesterday you left it up to me whether I would tender these statements or not and I am now tendering these statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Have we ever looked at those documents -- statement at all? Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the statements are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Referred to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: They're referred to. Their content is irrelevant to these proceedings. I put two propositions to Professor Dunjic that he changed his opinion on the significance of civilian clothes and winter clothes, and I think he's explained, both to me and to Mr. Karadzic, the reason for those differences. So I don't know that the underlying statements provide any further clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that points have been already made, I wonder whether we need to admit it separately. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, these statements do corroborate what he said, so if there's any doubt about the fact, they're corroborated by the statement. But if there's no dispute about that, it's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I don't think there's any dispute. Professor Dunjic said one thing about civilian clothing in one statement, one thing about winter clothing, and it's different now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we leave it at that. In general, the Court -- the Chamber has some reservation cumulating a lot of documents. Thank you. Shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor Dunjic, did you come across data that there were ball bearings in the bodies which come from hand-grenades?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in a number of localities, I think this was Zeleni Jadar 5, I cannot remember the precise localities, but some ball bearings were found in some bodies from shot-guns but also from some other devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you know -- or actually, we saw from the material relating to San Antonio that there is awareness of the fact that there were wars in that place before Srebrenica. Even Dean Manning said in response to my question that there was some fighting that continued after Srebrenica. So not even Mr. Manning knows. Do you know the number of victims of the 28th Division before 1995? Line 3, it should say "nisu imali svest" There was no awareness.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have information which would indicate to me how many victims there were before July 1995 among the soldiers and civilians of the B&H army, but I know that there was fighting there before July, between 1992 and 1995, and that a large number was killed in that interval on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at 1D9323 in e-court, please. Unfortunately we don't have a translation. I think we don't have a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor, can you help us, does it say here above these tables --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like some showing of provenance of this document. It doesn't have an ERN by the looks of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is something that was seized on the computers in Zepa, their entire communications with the Main Staff of the 28th Division. The 28th Division had a computer full of these documents and this is one of those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'd object to any use of a document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we collapse --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- without an ERN and without --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Shall we collapse it for the moment. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'd object to any use of a document without an ERN and without a translation. We have absolutely no idea what this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, that would mean that only documents that were produced by the Prosecution could ever be shown to a witness. So we -- if the fact that it doesn't have an ERN isn't dispositive of that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: That's not what I was saying, Mr. President. It's the combination of not knowing where it came from and the lack of translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When the Chamber or the parties cannot be satisfied with the provenance, you object to the use of it. That's the point?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I object to the use of it until I have a translation so I can see what it is for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, that's not how we've been proceeding, Mr. President. So I think the document can be used. The issue of provenance will go to its admissibility, but nevertheless, we can proceed further than we have right now by allowing the witness to answer questions about the document. And if there's no adequate showing of provenance, it won't be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber tends to agree with Mr. Robinson's observation. Let's see how it evolves, whether the witness is able to make any comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please just confirm for us whether it says that this is an overview of casualties --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- of units in the 28th Division on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you ask the witness to read it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the heading and you can skip the rest until the title of the tables.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, allow me. I understood that the Judge was saying this. This is a report by the Army of Republika -- B&H sent to the command of the 28th Division, then we have the number, Srebrenica, the 3rd of April, 1995. And then the subheading is: "Report on losses of the 28th Division," and then there is a chunk of text. And then it says: "Overview of losses or casualties of units of the OGA on the 31st" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- "of December 1994" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think we should be jumping any chunks of text in this document. I think every word should be read out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not a problem for me at all to read it. I just thought I would cut the whole process short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Professor, could you read out the first sentence -- first line of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says at the top: Copy of -- not that. You mean this: "Armija, Army of the republic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not that one --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- of BiH.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're right, Mr. -- copy of something. It's in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- of the republic, military secret, strictly confidential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could concentrate on answering the question. Can you see the last page -- the last line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Last line of this document. Could you scroll down. The "page" is also English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Da, "page 1."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So could you explain to us what this document is about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you scroll up, please. This document, this is a report about military casualties of personnel of the unit A8, Army 8, on the 31st of December, 1994. So these are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, accepting --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- total casualties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Accepting that, why does that document have English words? Do you have any clue? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I think that I cannot finish before the break, so we will try to find the document in EDS with its ERN number, the same document. But these things in the computer were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- pre-programmed. That's the computer programme.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Shall we have a break for 45 minutes and resume at 1.20. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.36 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Some further information, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Two very short points, Mr. President. I withdraw my objection to the last document showed by Mr. Karadzic, 1D9323. We have a different version of the same document in our collection. We've uploaded that into e-court as 65 ter 22548 [sic] and there's been a draft translation done over lunch. So we can see at least the first part in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: The second point, Professor Wright testified at transcript 22268 about the Glogova L sub-grave appearing between the 17th and the 27th of July. And Your Honours may recall in the notification for Professor Wright which was filed on the 28th of November, 2011, we specifically withdrew -- there is a separate report that Professor Wright did on sub-grave L, we withdrew that report because the victims aren't associated with scheduled incident E-3.1 which is the Kravica warehouse killing. So Professor Wright quite -- or quite deliberately, we didn't lead evidence from Professor Wright on grave L because it's not associated with that schedule E incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, shall we use 22548 instead of this one?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid that it's 25458.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give the number again, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we're waiting, I just notice that we're sitting without Judge Lattanzi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Thank you for the reminder. She cannot be with us due to her official functions until the end of today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, may we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told that we have some draft translation. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you confirm, Professor, that this is also the 31st December and that the heading and everything else is identical?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the document in question, 3rd of April, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the following page in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's all we have, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The table has not been translated, just the text. Can we then go to the last page in the Serbian language. Five pages are missing. ERN numbers are 1375 plus six or five pages. 1380 or 1381 are missing, and in the previous version the whole document was there in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I've no objection if Mr. Karadzic wants to use his B/C/S version with this English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Fair enough. Shall we go back to the document 1D9323.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we go to the penultimate page, the last is of no consequence, the penultimate page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor, could I please ask you to look at the totals. The columns are: Killed, slightly wounded, seriously wounded, total losses. How many were killed before the 1st of January, 1995?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this table that you have just shown me, the total number of killed was 1607, 1.607. Among the group of seriously wounded there was 654. Among the group slightly wounded, there were 2.501. Total losses, 4.762, and those who went missing, 225. 1.607 killed; and 225 missing; seriously wounded, 654; slightly wounded, 2.501, this is on page 11 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, the documents that you perused, did they differentiate between the casualties among the 28th -- the 128th [as interpreted] Division and those that were inflicted in July of 1995, was there a difference?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not come across such a document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document. Can the document be completed, both the English and Serbian versions thereof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, no objection.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI D3897, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor, sir, a big thank you for your effort and the work that you have done and thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. That concludes your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank you for your patience. Some answers may have been a bit lengthy, but I thought that it was necessary for me to clarify things to make everybody understand what I wrote about. Thank you. May I go now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. Nicholls, you have some matters to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Actually, having looked at the issue again, I don't have a preliminary. We can just continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next we are going to hear the cross-examination of Mr. Keserovic, whose examination-in-chief was concluded .

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I need just one minute for the computer to boot up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How are you, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would like to advise you that your solemn declaration that you made previously is still in effect. And today we'll continue with the cross-examination by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. You understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Professor.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The first thing I wanted to ask you about is some of your testimony that we heard a couple weeks ago and parts of your report it's related to. I'm first referring to your report - you don't need to look at it now - for the parties at page 22, para 14, and Mr. Brown's report para 2.81 and paras 2.92 to 2.98, specifically regarding the situation in Vecici, Kotor Varos. You remember talking about that in your report and in your testimony here?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now at T 40939, Mr. Karadzic asked you about Mr. Brown's analysis of what he called the case of Vecici, and you testified at 40940: "Quite simply, disarming is a basic prerequisite for any disarming and any such actions, and as a result, a lot of conflicts took place in which many residents of Vecici perished. "Q. Did Mr. Brown observe that out of all the many Muslim and Croat villages, it was only the village of Vecici that clashed and suffered as many victims?" And you said: "Well, I did say that Mr. Brown analysed this particular locality only, and this incident involving Vecici where there were quite a few casualties is presented without any analysis, et cetera, which led to the conflict where they actually perished." So I want to talk a moment about the casualties in Vecici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 65 ter 00719, please. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, this is a combat report, 1 KK combat report, 4 November 1992. It's cited in Mr. Brown's report at 443 and 740 footnotes. And it states: "Green Berets pulling out of Vecici village fell into our ambush. Forty of them were killed during the clash and another 20 members of the so-called BH army were captured. Another 150 members of Green Berets, mostly women and children, surrendered in the evening hours ..." You seen this report before? Did they give it to you? It's cited in Mr. Brown's report.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I saw all of the report. I am not sure that I saw all of its paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Well, we gave the Defence a hyper-linked CD, I believe, with all of his documents and his footnotes linked to it. Did they give that to you when you were preparing your critique?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received documents from the Defence. Those are the documents that Mr. Brown refers to in his conclusions, i.e., in his comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, did you receive all of the documents that Mr. Brown footnotes in his report, yes, no, or you don't know, or you don't remember?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those that are mentioned in footnotes, I believe that I have been provided with those documents, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So you had this one and this talks about 40 -- 40 members -- 40 casualties and it's talking about Vecici in November; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender that, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6462, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just before we move on, clearly this is sent to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 00293.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is also 4 November, also from the 1 KK, also to the Main Staff. And this is at Brown's footnote 445. And if you look at paragraph 2, do you remember seeing this document? You remember this one, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the document contains the same information as the previous one. The contents are virtually the same. Only the sequence of paragraphs is different. However, what is mentioned --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Wait a minute, wait a minute --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- under bullet point 2 again refers to Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Just in case my question wasn't clear, what I was asking you was: Do you remember seeing this document? Do you remember this document when you were preparing your report?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you're right, the content is similar and it's related, but let's look at what it says in paragraph 2 -- section 2, rather. "In the area of Kotor Varos, there was a clash between members of the Muslim forces and our units, because of the refusal to negotiate on moving out of the Vecici village area. About 40 Green Beret members were killed and about 200 were captured. A brutal massacre of the captured members of the Green Berets started because of the wounding of four and killing of one soldier of the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade, and the burning of wounded soldiers on Gola Planina (Jajce). "Measures to prevent further massacre were taken through the 22nd Light Infantry Brigade." So this also says that 40 members of the enemy were killed in combat because one soldier was killed and four wounded and the -- and it states that the brutal massacre of prisoners started. This is also sent to the Main Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender that, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have any objection, but so far all that's been established from these two documents is that they say what they say they say. I think if there's some substance to this cross-examination, he ought to be allowed to comment on it or some question ought to be asked about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I expect some to be coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm going to show him one more document and then, having put these three chain of related documents together, ask him to comment. So again, I would tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6463, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now if I could have 65 ter 00722, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is from the next day, also from the 1 KK, also to the Main Staff, situation on the territory in paragraph 4. "The situation in Kotor Varos municipality is still very complex. After they refused to return the weapons and surrender to the Army of Republika Srpska, Muslim extremists from the village of Vecici attempted to fight their way through towards Travnik. "In the clash against the Army of Republika Srpska, following the death of one soldier and the wounding of several others, more than 150 extremists died in combat." Now, this document also says one soldier killed and several wounded, but now it says 150 deaths in combat, and that's no way correct, is it? There weren't 150 deaths in combat. This is a sanitised report of the massacre, isn't it? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says unambiguously here that over 150 extremists were killed in fighting, and I can tell only based on what I read whether they were really killed in fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, how many times have you seen 150 combatants killed in one day of fighting and how many times have you seen one report that says after one soldier was killed and four wounded, a brutal massacre started, and then another report saying after one soldier was killed and several wounded, 150 were killed in combat?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not commonplace. I don't remember that I ever saw so many people being killed in combat in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. Now, when you were answering Dr. Karadzic's question, you talked about casualties and he talked about the case of Vecici. If people are killed in a brutal massacre, they aren't casualties, are they; they're victims?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I did not analyse the way those people died. I did not establish the number of deaths nor did I analyse how that was done. I just provided my opinion about Mr. Karadzic's position as well as the commanders primarily of the 1st Corps. When Vecici was blockaded and when negotiations started --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- they thought that the civilian population should be protected --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that. That's what you talked about in your report. What I'm talking about is in your testimony here when you talked about casualties and you had this document available to you, you said you didn't analyse how it occurred. So in your expert testimony to the Trial Chamber, calling these casualties, you didn't point out that there was also a document which referred to these deaths as the victims of a brutal massacre?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is possible that I did not talk about the manner of death and the number of those who died. I focused more on the attitude of the Serbian side towards the issue of Vecici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll talk a bit more in a minute about the issue of punishment in the 1 KK for soldiers who committed crimes. But before we get to that, are you aware of anybody being prosecuted for the Vecici massacre, either in your personal experience since you were at the 1 -- well, you weren't at the 1 KK at that point, either from your personal experience or from your research?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the 1 KK, the military court and the military prosecutor initiated proceedings and conducted investigations against some individuals who had participated in those events. I don't know anything about the epilogues of those activities, I didn't analyse them. I don't know how that all ended up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So the answer is -- this is November 1992, this is when the military courts had been running for some time, the Banja Luka military courts. You're not able to point me to any prosecution during the war for 1 KK soldiers for this crime; right? That's what you just said?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For Vecici, no, nothing for Vecici, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Let me just look at what you said a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender that, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6464, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, you just said at page 80, line 1: "In the 1 KK, the military court and the military prosecutor initiated proceedings and conducted investigations against some individuals who had participated in those events. I don't know anything about the -- of those activities, I didn't analyse them. I don't know how all that ended up." That's what you just said. Let me tell you what it says in your report, page 20 of the English: "Many actions which we have mentioned were taken systematically so that subordinate personnel would not commit criminal or other offences against non-Serbs, and when they did occur, the perpetrators were arrested and criminally prosecuted." And this is what you said at T 40955 when you testified here on direct: "I repeat that he," and here you were speaking of the 1 KK command, "gave priority to incidents and criminal offences that undoubtedly did happen, but that was not prevalent conduct and they had never been encouraged or ordered by anyone. And if they happened, they always ended up by discovering the perpetrators and prosecuting them or applying appropriate measures against them." So my question is: How could you testify last week that these cases always ended up by discovering the perpetrators and prosecuting them, when - as you say today - you didn't analyse those cases and you don't know how they turned out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I don't know specifically how those cases relative to Vecici ended. I don't know the individuals, I don't know the epilogue, how many persons and what measures were taken. But I said that I knew that judiciary bodies did conduct proceedings relative to that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You said: "If they happened, they always ended up by discovering the perpetrators and prosecuting them," that's what you said, speaking about these incidents generally. Do you stand by that now, that these crimes were always prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Proceedings were always conducted. Those people were processed and those proceedings ended in one way or another. I don't know of any major or more significant crimes that were committed that were discovered and that were not prosecuted by the judiciary bodies in 1 KK. They always conducted investigations and took measures in order to deal with such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I'll put it to you, and it's impossible to prove this negative at the moment, that nobody was arrested or prosecuted for the Vecici killings. If you know the name of somebody who was prosecuted or a case number or anything like that, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that I didn't know names.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that the victims of that killing, their bodies have still not been found? Did you know that? They're still missing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the material that I analysed and in the process itself, I encountered data that a number of those people, or rather, victims were not found. Therefore, yes, I knew that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's talk about another crime quickly, another major notorious crime. This one was -- occurred approximately 16 days before you arrived at the 1 KK. You arrived on 17 June 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 17th of June, 1992, at the Army of Republika Srpska, and at the 1st Krajina Corps on the 21st of June of the same year.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And let's look at this event just over two weeks before you arrived. Have you heard about the mass killing at the Velagici school in Kljuc which took place on June 1st, 1992, in which 80 civilians were murdered in the school?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear of the event at the Velagici school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you agree with me it was the murder of 80 civilians; right? Approximately 80, might not know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would need to look at the document. There are reports which state the precise number. There are many documents. I don't know all the numbers of -- by -- just like that. But I know that there was an incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we can agree that this incident is a mass killing of Muslims, right, by VRS soldiers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is this incident another example of your testimony that the perpetrators were always discovered and prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reports, or rather, this incident or crime was not concealed. It was reported on through regular channels and measures were ordered for the perpetrators to be found and processed. I would like to emphasise once again that I did not analyse either the numbers of those killed, nor did I deny in any way that criminal acts occurred. But I spoke and emphasised that this was never the official policy, either of the authorities or of the Army of Republika Srpska, and that always in every place they ordered and emphasised the protection and the respect of all, protection primarily, first of all, of the civilian population, of prisoners of war, and the adherence to the laws and customs of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. But that's not all you said. What you've also testified to is what I've quoted about three times, that they always ended up by discovering the perpetrators and prosecuting them. Now, you will agree with me that in this case the perpetrators were discovered because everybody knew who they were but they weren't prosecuted, that the 1 KK military courts let them go.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, in this case and in cases in general that have to do with incidents in the territory of the Kljuc municipality, since this refers to that municipality, proceedings were conducted, perpetrators were found and arrested. As for whether they were released later or not, that was the decision of the court. But today we still have persons who took part in these events who are serving prison sentences of several years in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Proceedings were conducted, proceedings are conducted now before courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. So we'll move on to this, but the reason they're serving their sentences now, their eight-year sentences, of that about length, like the murder of Omer Filipovic, the reason they're serving their sentences now is because they weren't prosecuted until after 2000; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war they were not all -- without doubt, not all of them were sentenced then and sent to serve their sentence. But the proceedings were conducted. As for the way they ended is something that is for a different type of analysis that I did not do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I don't want to belabour this, but you do analyse this because you said to this Court that people were always captured and prosecuted and you did that in relation to showing how the 1 KK and the authorities did their job. So is your view that the 1 KK is doing its job and all it can to prevent crime and the RS authorities are doing all they can to prevent crime in 1992 when the perpetrator is punished by a civilian court in 2006? That goes to the credit of the 1 KK?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Krajina Corps and the authorities, without doubt, did everything to prevent any perpetration of crimes in the AOR of the corps, unnecessary killings or anything else. And they ordered that measures be taken against the perpetrators. These were the documents that I cited in my findings. The 1st Corps did not issue a single document without in particular emphasising the protection of all, emphasising that this should be done without regard to ethnic, religious, or any other kind of affiliation --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in such circumstances --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you because we're not talking about prophylactic orders before the crimes happening. What I'm talking to you about now is what happens after the 1 KK soldiers commit mass murders. You tell me of one Serb soldier case that you know of convicted during the war, other than Stankovic, for crimes committed against Muslims or Croats, murders?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it is beyond the expertise. This is something that should be put to the president of the court, Novak Todorovic. He was available to the Prosecution and he did state this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did he not deal with this part in his evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He did, Your Honours. That's the part I've quoted about four times, that everybody was punished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's a fair question. Can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are examples. While preparing and speaking only with two judges from that time, the military tribunal in Banja Luka, Nikola Tomasevic and Srdjan Forca, they stated that each one of them individually reached -- or passed, handed down a number of convictions against Serbs for atrocities against Muslims or Croats. Among them was also one death sentence which was commuted later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. You know about the Velagici massacre, you heard about that. You tell me, do you know if anybody was prosecuted for that crime during the war at all, even though all 12 suspects were known? By "prosecuted" -- let me rephrase that. Strike that. You tell me if anybody was convicted of that crime which occurred in June 1992, before the end of the war, when those men stayed serving in their units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that question, whether anyone was convicted. I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we can move on, but then I think you'll agree with me that your statement last time you testified here - and I'm not accusing you of anything - but when you said that the perpetrators were always identified and everybody was convicted and punished, words to that effect, that in fact you were wrong?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I said that all were convicted, but I did say that proceedings were conducted and I stand by that, that every case that was discovered, for every such case orders were issued that perpetrators be found and that proceedings be initiated against them and that they should be held responsible for that. I said that, but as for the final outcome, whether everybody was convicted and sent to serve their sentence, I don't think that I said anything like that in that form. I said that proceedings were conducted and that appropriate orders for that were issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What you said was at T 4095 [sic]: "I repeat, he gave priority to incidents and criminal offences that undoubtedly did happen, but that was not prevalent conduct and they had never been encouraged and ordered by anyone. And if they happened, they always ended up by discovering the perpetrators and prosecuting them or applying appropriate measures against them." So by "prosecute," if they just take a criminal report and then send the soldiers back to the front, you include that in your statement, right, as "prosecuting"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Criminal proceedings, yes, launching an investigation in terms of finding the perpetrators and conducting the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me move on to something else that you feature in your testimony. You testified to the effect that wherever the army was involved, it prevented inter-ethnic conflicts and that everybody felt safer when the JNA was there. That's at 40956, that everyone felt safer when the JNA was there. And at T 4095 [sic] you were asked: "General, was the army involved in preventing inter-ethnic conflicts and did that have a negative effect on the combat-readiness of the corps and its units? Was that something that Mr. Brown noticed, that certain elements were allocated to prevent such conflicts?" And you answered: "Throughout the whole period and especially 1992, elements of units and even entire units were involved in the activities and the internal areas surrounded by front lines. They established organs and regimens and situations that would provide protection for the population living in the area ..." And little bit further you said: "The sole purpose was to make the area more peaceful and safer. After all, the people everywhere including in Bosnia-Herzegovina felt safer if they had army units deployed in certain areas." You remember saying that; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did write about this without doubt. I don't know whether that is the way you said it word for word, but the gist of it is what you have said, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have P03660, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: While that's coming up, did you know Branko Basara personally by any chance? The 6th Krajina Corps commander -- the 6th Krajina Brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war, or rather, at that time I did not know him. I met him several years after the war personally in a brief meeting. So no, we did not know each other personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Well, this is his war record, his handwritten war record of the 6th Infantry Brigade, his brigade in Sanski Most. And just so you know, in an interview with the OTP he confirmed that this was his handwriting, that he wrote this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I'd like to go to section 4 which is on page 2 of the English. It should be page 3 of the Serbian original.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, and if you -- it may be difficult to read, but if you can read section 4 is the part I'm going to be directing you to, where Mr. Basara, writing the history of his brigade, says: "On 3rd April 91," that's the way it's written, should be 92, "the 6th was transferred in complete order and with utmost secrecy from Jasenovac to the area of Sanski Most so that everyone was surprised. With the arrival of the brigade on this territory, the Muslims and Croats became afraid, and the Serbs heaved a sign -- a sigh of relief." Now, it's not a huge point, but Basara was there, he arrived in Sanski Most. You said everybody felt safer when there were there and they were there to prevent inter-ethnic conflicts. When the 6th Brigade showed up in Sanski Most, Muslims and Croats became frightened and the Serbs gained confidence; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that with the arrival of the brigade, the Muslims and the Croats became afraid and the Serbs heaved a sigh of relief. What the reason was and how Basara experienced this, I must say I did not have the opportunity to see this document before now. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, excuse me --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I would --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- sorry, continue. I'm sorry, continue. I shouldn't have interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I don't remember seeing this document in handwriting the way we see it here, but undoubtedly, in 1991, already in the Sanski Most area, among other places, paramilitary organising of Muslims and Croats took place. I emphasise paramilitary because at that time in 1991 until May 1992, the only legal armed force in that area was the Yugoslav People's Army. There was illegal arming, and the fear of Muslims and Croats could have also been due to the reason that they were organising in a paramilitary way, they were illegally obtaining weaponry, and they were preparing, without doubt, for conflict and did not have anyone else to go into conflict with other than the Serbs in that area. And why did the Serbs heave a sigh of relief? The Serbs responded to the call of the federal state and the then-JNA, they were mobilised and took part in the resolution of problems that were there in the Republic of Croatia. Their families stayed behind in Sanski Most literally without protection. And now when the brigade returned, it was normal that they heaved a sigh of relief and that they felt a bit better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, well, first of all, you said this wasn't available to you. It was available to you as Ewan Brown's footnote 132, just for the record. Let me look at another part of what Mr. Basara writes in his history. He says: "Since our task as a JNA unit was to prevent conflicts between the nationalities, that is, to prevent the slaughter of the Serbian people, we could not publicly arm the Serbs. We then worked along the two lines: First, organising and arming the Serbian people, and second ... persuading the Muslims and Croats to remain loyal and that we could live together ..." So this does support Ewan Brown's two-track theory which he discussed and you criticised in your report and in your testimony, doesn't it? I won't go through this entire part of this, but you can see Basara writes about how they employed tricks to arm the Serbs legally and the Serbs only.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
